stem: You need to list pods from all namespaces. Which command does this correctly?
rationale: The flag you need is `-A` (all namespaces). There is no namespace called "all".

stem: A pod will not start. Which command shows its recent events?
rationale: `describe` shows events, and they usually explain why the pod was not scheduled to a node or did not start. For `logs` to work, the container must already have started.

stem: Which command lists all resource types available in the cluster?
rationale: `kubectl api-resources` lists every resource type the cluster serves, including Cozystack's own types.

stem: Which object maintains the desired number of pod replicas?
rationale: A ReplicaSet (created by a Deployment) makes sure the declared number of pod replicas is running.

stem: A service on bare metal in Cozystack needs an external IP. Which Service type requests one?
rationale: The LoadBalancer type requests an external IP. On bare metal in Cozystack, these addresses are assigned by MetalLB.

stem: How does a virtual machine run in Cozystack?

options.text: On a separate hypervisor cluster outside Kubernetes
As a Kubernetes pod managed by KubeVirt
As a systemd service on the node

rationale: KubeVirt runs each VM inside a pod (via QEMU), so a VM is an ordinary Kubernetes workload.

stem: Which manifest field defines the desired state of an object?
rationale: The desired state is declared in `spec`. `metadata` holds the object's identity, while `kind` and `apiVersion` define its type.

stem: Which command validates a manifest without creating anything?
rationale: `--dry-run=server` sends the manifest to the API server for validation but does not persist anything.

stem: A managed application in Cozystack (a database, for example) has generated connection credentials. Where will it put them?

options.text: In a ConfigMap in the platform namespace
In a generated Secret in the tenant namespace

rationale: Managed applications expose credentials through generated Secrets. The tenant kubeconfig is also assembled from a Secret (module M2).

stem: What is a Helm release?

options.text: A version of the Helm binary
A single instance of a chart installed in the cluster
A Git tag in the chart repository

rationale: A release is a single installed instance of a chart. One chart can produce many releases with different values.

stem: What does the `--install` flag add to the `helm upgrade` command?

options.text: Forces all pods to be reinstalled
Installs the release if it does not exist yet
Upgrades all releases in the cluster

rationale: `upgrade --install` is idempotent: if the release does not exist, it installs it; if it exists, it upgrades it.

stem: What does the READY column in the output of `kubectl get hr -A` tell you?

options.text: Whether the pod images have been pulled
Whether the HelmRelease has been reconciled and is healthy
Whether pods can be scheduled on the node
Whether the Git repository is reachable

rationale: READY True means the HelmRelease has been reconciled to the desired state and is healthy. If it is False, check the MESSAGE column and `kubectl describe hr`.

stem: What happens when a HelmRelease is suspended?

options.text: The controller stops reconciling it, and manual changes are kept
The chart is removed from the repository
The namespace is locked for all users

rationale: Suspend stops reconciliation, so manual changes stay in place. Resume hands control back to the declared state.

stem: What is the correct order of Cozystack layers, from bottom to top?
rationale: Talos is the node operating system, Kubernetes (the management cluster) runs on top of it, and the Cozystack platform is installed on Kubernetes.

stem: In what form does Cozystack expose platform objects such as tenants, virtual machines and so on?

options.text: Through a separate proprietary API server unrelated to Kubernetes
As rows in an internal SQL database

rationale: Cozystack extends Kubernetes with custom resources. The dashboard and Terraform are just other clients of the same Kubernetes API.

stem: How does an operator change the configuration of a Talos node?

options.text: Logs in over SSH and edits files
Applies a declarative machine configuration through the Talos API
Uses a package manager on the node
Edits the root file system from a rescue shell

rationale: Talos has no SSH, and the root file system is read-only. The only way is a declarative machine configuration applied through the Talos API.

stem: Why does Cozystack ship its own Talos image?

options.text: To add an SSH server for debugging
To include the DRBD and ZFS kernel modules the platform needs
To replace kubelet with its own agent
To reduce the licence cost of stock Talos

rationale: The platform needs the DRBD (for LINSTOR storage) and ZFS kernel modules, and the stock Talos image does not include them.

stem: Which tool does Cozystack recommend for deploying Kubernetes on Talos?
rationale: Talm is Cozystack's own Talos configuration manager with Helm-style templating. It is the path the documentation describes as recommended.

stem: In a PXE installation, two components run as temporary Docker containers. Which pair?
rationale: In a PXE installation, temporary containers run Matchbox (serves the Talos image over HTTP) and dnsmasq (DHCP + TFTP).

stem: How do you confirm that a Cozystack installation succeeded?

options.text: `kubectl get nodes` shows all nodes as Ready
`kubectl get hr -A` shows all HelmReleases as READY

rationale: The documentation gives a single success criterion: in `kubectl get hr -A`, every platform HelmRelease shows READY True.

stem: A team needs the full Cozystack feature set, but its nodes run RKE2 rather than Talos. Which variant fits?
rationale: `isp-full-generic` provides the full feature set on standard distributions (k3s, kubeadm, RKE2) instead of Talos.

stem: Which variant is installed on top of an existing managed Kubernetes cluster and comes **without** CNI, storage and virtualization?
rationale: `isp-hosted` runs on a ready-made managed Kubernetes cluster where CNI, storage and virtualization (if any) are already provided by the provider.

stem: What does the `default` variant include?

options.text: A full PaaS stack with monitoring
Only PackageSources, without a ready-made set of components
Only the dashboard and the API
A demo tenant with sample applications

rationale: The `default` variant installs only PackageSources; the administrator enables each component manually (the BYOP approach).

stem: How are platform packages named?
rationale: Platform packages follow the `cozystack.<component>` naming scheme; `kubectl get package` lists them.

stem: When can a platform package be disabled through `bundles.disabledPackages`?

options.text: At any time; the platform will remove the component itself
Before installation; afterwards it has to be removed manually with Helm
Never; the set of packages is fixed by the variant

rationale: Disabling works before installation. A component that is already installed has to be removed manually with Helm; the platform will not do it for you.

stem: Which component reconciles all of the platform's HelmReleases?
rationale: FluxCD is the GitOps engine. Every platform component is described as a HelmRelease, and FluxCD continuously reconciles them against the desired state.

stem: Which component runs the control planes of tenant Kubernetes clusters as pods in the management cluster?
rationale: Kamaji runs the control planes of tenant Kubernetes clusters as pods inside the management cluster.

stem: Which component provides replicated block storage for persistent volumes?
rationale: LINSTOR manages replicated DRBD block volumes. SeaweedFS is object storage, Velero is backups.

stem: What is the minimum cluster configuration described in the documentation for a dev/lab installation?

options.text: 3 nodes, each with 8 cores / 24 GB RAM / 50 GB + 256 GB disks
6 nodes, each with 32 cores / 128 GB RAM
2 nodes, each with 16 cores / 64 GB RAM

rationale: The documented minimum is 3 nodes with 8 cores and 24 GB RAM each and two disks: 50 GB for the system and 256 GB for data.

stem: Which network condition is strongly discouraged for a Cozystack cluster?

options.text: All nodes in a single L2 segment
nip.io as the platform FQDN in a lab

rationale: The latency requirement is an RTT below 10 ms. Running above 20 ms is strongly discouraged, and such a configuration is not supported.

stem: What is the primary unit of isolation in Cozystack?
rationale: The Tenant resource is a "namespace with extended capabilities" and the primary unit of isolation in the platform.

stem: How does a tenant administrator create a nested tenant?

options.text: By filing a request with the platform team
By creating a Tenant resource, like any application from the catalog
With a command through the Talos API

rationale: A Tenant is itself an application from the catalog. A nested tenant is created as a Tenant resource in the parent's namespace.

stem: Tenant `beta` is nested in tenant `alpha`, which is nested in the root tenant. Which namespace will `beta` get?
rationale: The chain of ancestors accumulates, but the root tenant is not repeated in the name: root/alpha/beta gives tenant-alpha-beta.

stem: Why are hyphens not allowed in tenant names?

options.text: Kubernetes does not allow hyphens in resource names
The hyphen separates ancestors in the namespace name
A hyphen breaks the username format in Keycloak

rationale: Hyphens separate ancestor names in the derived namespace. A hyphen inside a tenant name would make the chain of ancestors ambiguous.

stem: Where in a tenant resource do you find the tenant's own namespace?
rationale: `metadata.namespace` holds the parent's namespace, which is where the resource itself lives. `status.namespace` is the namespace the platform created for this tenant.

stem: Which label allows a pod to reach the Kubernetes apiserver inside a tenant?
rationale: Access is enabled explicitly with the `policy.cozystack.io/allow-to-apiserver: "true"` label, which is set on each pod individually.

stem: How do you disable tenant network isolation in v1.5?

options.text: Set `isolated: false` in the Tenant resource
Delete the Cilium network policies manually
You can't: isolation has been mandatory since v1.0

rationale: The `isolated` flag was removed in v1.0. Isolation is mandatory and cannot be disabled.

stem: Which component enforces tenant network isolation?
rationale: The isolating network policies are generated automatically and enforced by Cilium's eBPF data plane.

stem: Which set lists the tenant-level service toggles?
rationale: The Tenant resource has exactly four such toggles: etcd, monitoring, ingress and seaweedfs.

stem: Tenant `beta` inside `alpha` does not have monitoring enabled, while `alpha` has `monitoring: true`. Where will beta's metrics go?

options.text: Nowhere: monitoring is disabled for beta
Always to the root tenant's stack

rationale: A missing service is inherited from the nearest ancestor that runs it. Here that is the parent alpha, not necessarily the root.

stem: Which preset series has a CPU-to-RAM ratio of 1:4?
rationale: Preset ratios: t1=1:0.5, c1=1:1, s1=1:2, u1=1:4, m1=1:8. So 1:4 is u1. (This is about tenant and application presets, not VM instance types.)

stem: With the default `cpuAllocationRatio` = 10, how much CPU will a workload with a 2 CPU limit request from the scheduler?
rationale: The request is the limit divided by cpuAllocationRatio: 2 / 10 = 0.2 CPU.

stem: A manifest specifies both a preset and an explicit `resources: {cpu, memory}` block. Which one takes effect?

options.text: The preset; the explicit resources are ignored
The explicit resources; they override the preset
Neither; the manifest will be rejected
The larger of the two values for each field

rationale: Explicit values in `resources: {cpu, memory}` always take precedence over the selected preset.

stem: What does the script from the documentation build a tenant kubeconfig from?

options.text: The token and CA certificate in the tenant secret, plus the server address from the administrator's kubeconfig

rationale: The script from the documentation reads the tenant's secret of the same name and takes the token (the token field), the CA certificate (ca.crt) and the default namespace from it. The API server address is not in the secret: the script fills it in from the current kubeconfig of the administrator who runs the script.

stem: The platform domain is `cloud.example.com`. Which default domain will tenant `alpha` under the root get?
rationale: A tenant's default domain is built as `<name>.<parent domain>`, so alpha under the root gets `alpha.cloud.example.com`.

stem: Which catalog group does **Qdrant** belong to?
rationale: Qdrant is a vector database, so it belongs in the databases group.

stem: Which operator manages PostgreSQL in Cozystack?
rationale: Managed PostgreSQL is handled by CloudNativePG. Strimzi is Kafka, Percona is MongoDB, Altinity is ClickHouse.

stem: How does a tenant administrator create a nested tenant?

options.text: By filing a request with the platform team
By deploying the Tenant application from the catalog
By creating a Kubernetes namespace directly

rationale: A Tenant is itself an application from the catalog. A nested tenant is deployed inside the parent tenant just like any other application.

stem: Which API group do catalog application resources live in?
rationale: All catalog applications are custom resources in the `apps.cozystack.io/v1alpha1` group.

stem: You have created a `Postgres` resource. What will the platform create as the next link in the chain?

options.text: A HelmRelease that installs the application's chart

rationale: The chain is: resource → HelmRelease (FluxCD) → Helm chart → operator → running workload.

stem: Which command shows all catalog application types available in the cluster?
rationale: `kubectl api-resources | grep apps.cozystack` lists all catalog types the platform serves.

stem: What does the Cozystack dashboard create when you deploy an application through a form?

options.text: A shell script on the control node
The same custom resource as `kubectl apply`
A snapshot of the tenant namespace

rationale: The dashboard works directly with the Kubernetes API: the form creates exactly the same resource you would apply with kubectl.

stem: Where do the application forms in the dashboard come from?

options.text: They are generated from the application resource schemas
Frontend developers write them by hand for each application
They are configured in the Platform Package
They are imported from Terraform modules

rationale: the dashboard is schema-driven: forms are generated from the application resource schemas, so the UI and the API never diverge.

stem: A team keeps all its infrastructure in Terraform and wants to describe Cozystack databases in the same codebase. What is the simplest way to do this?

options.text: Click through the dashboard and write the steps down in the documentation
Use the Cozystack Terraform provider or `kubernetes_manifest` resources
Write a cron job that calls kubectl

rationale: the official Terraform provider (or a plain kubernetes_manifest resource) manages the same CRs as code.

stem: What happens if you run `kubectl delete` on a `Postgres` application CR?

options.text: Only the CR object is deleted; the database keeps running
The application is deleted together with its workloads
The command fails: applications can only be deleted from the dashboard
The database is automatically archived to S3

rationale: deleting an application CR removes the whole application, pods and data included. Treat it like DROP DATABASE.

stem: Which set of applications gained TLS support in Cozystack v1.5?

options.text: VPN, TCP Balancer, HTTP Cache, VPC

rationale: in v1.5, TLS arrived for Kafka, NATS, Qdrant and PostgreSQL; databases exposed externally get TLS automatically.

stem: What is an ApplicationDefinition for?

options.text: To set resource quotas for a tenant
To add a new application type to the catalog based on a Helm chart
To describe an application's network policy
To pin the platform to a specific version

rationale: ApplicationDefinition registers a new application type in the catalog based on a Helm chart, with its own CR kind and dashboard form.

stem: What does the `cozy-default` BackupClass provide in v1.5?

options.text: Automatic snapshots of all virtual machines
Working backups of managed applications out of the box, to a shared system S3 bucket
A full copy of the management cluster
Incremental block-level copies of virtual machines

rationale: cozy-default is a ready-made BackupClass wired to a shared system S3 bucket (the full model is in M6).

stem: How does KubeVirt run a virtual machine?

options.text: On a separate hypervisor cluster next to Kubernetes
Inside a Kubernetes pod, as a qemu process
As a WebAssembly module inside the kubelet
Inside a Docker-in-Docker container on the control plane

rationale: KubeVirt runs each VM as a qemu/KVM process inside a pod, so a VM is an ordinary Kubernetes workload.

stem: What role does CDI play in the virtualization stack?

options.text: It schedules virtual machine pods onto nodes
It provides a VNC console for virtual machines
It loads disk images into persistent volumes
It replicates disks between data centers

rationale: CDI (Containerized Data Importer) populates PVCs with disk images, from URLs, registries or uploads, through DataVolume objects.

stem: Which statement about virtual machines in Cozystack is true?

options.text: Tenant quotas do not apply to VMs
VMs are placed by the standard Kubernetes scheduler

rationale: since a VM is a pod, it is placed by the standard scheduler, and quotas and network policies apply to it as to any other workload.

stem: What is the correct way to create a virtual machine in Cozystack v1.5?

options.text: Create a single VirtualMachine resource with the disk inside
First create a VMDisk, then a VMInstance that references it
First create a VMInstance; the platform will create the disks itself
Create a DataVolume and a Pod by hand

rationale: the standard v1.5 model is two CRs, disk first: a VMDisk (storage), then a VMInstance that references it.

stem: Why are the disk and the instance separate resources?

options.text: Kubernetes cannot store two specs in one object
A disk has its own lifecycle: data survives deletion of the instance, and disks can be reused
Disks and instances must live in different namespaces
Live migration does not work otherwise

rationale: the whole point is separate lifecycles: the disk survives deletion of the instance, can be attached again and backed up on its own.

stem: A team wants every new VM to start from the same prepared Ubuntu image without downloading it each time. What should they use?

options.text: A VMImage (golden image) as the disk source
Uploading the image from a shared laptop

rationale: VMImage is exactly the golden image: you publish it once and then clone disks from it via source.image.name.

stem: A Linux machine has booted, but its network is misconfigured and SSH does not work. Which way can you still reach it?

options.text: The file manager in the dashboard

rationale: the serial console does not depend on the network inside the guest; it is the access path of last resort.

stem: What does cloud-init do?

options.text: Configures the guest OS on first boot: users, SSH keys, packages
Places the virtual machine pod on a node

rationale: cloud-init runs on first boot inside the guest and configures users, keys, hostname and packages.

stem: Which capability actually exists in Cozystack v1.5?

options.text: Automatic VM restart after a host failure (like vSphere HA)
Continuous automatic VM balancing across nodes (like DRS)
Live migration of running VMs between nodes
Incremental VM backups via changed block tracking

rationale: live migration exists; HA auto-restart, DRS balancing and CBT backups are honest gaps in v1.5.

stem: A team asks: “If a node dies, will our VMs restart on another one by themselves?” What is the honest answer for v1.5?

options.text: Yes, KubeVirt will bring them up within seconds
No: there is no fencing-based auto-restart out of the box, and recovery involves manual steps
Yes, but only for Windows guests

rationale: v1.5 has no fencing-based auto-restart; recovering VMs after a node failure involves manual steps.

stem: What changed in GPU passthrough in v1.5?

options.text: GPUs can no longer be attached to VMs
Node preparation was automated: labeling GPU nodes and binding devices
GPU passthrough now requires a commercial licence
GPUs are shared between VMs by default

rationale: v1.5 automated GPU node preparation: applying labels and binding devices to vfio-pci; the VMInstance itself requests GPUs through the gpus field.

stem: Which component provides network isolation between tenants in Cozystack?
rationale: Cilium enforces the automatically generated network policies that isolate tenants (M2).

stem: A pod inside a tenant needs to talk to the Kubernetes API server. What is required?

options.text: Nothing; API access is open by default
Set `isolated: false` in the Tenant resource

rationale: access to the API server is closed by default; a pod requests it explicitly with the label `policy.cozystack.io/allow-to-apiserver: "true"`.

stem: What does Kube-OVN add to the platform?

options.text: Persistent pod IP addresses when pods move between nodes

rationale: centralized IPAM in Kube-OVN keeps a pod's IP across rescheduling; the other options are about TenantGateway/cert-manager, Cilium and ExternalDNS.

stem: Why are persistent IP addresses especially important for virtual machines?

options.text: Kubernetes forbids pods from changing IPs
Workloads inside the guest, firewall rules and licences are often tied to a fixed IP

rationale: guest systems, firewall rules and licences are often bound to an IP; a VM that changes its address on every migration would break all of that.

stem: A colleague asks which of the two CNIs is responsible for what. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Cilium: overlay network and IPAM; Kube-OVN: network policies
Cilium: policies and Services (eBPF); Kube-OVN: overlay network, centralized IPAM, persistent IPs, VPC
Both layers do the same thing for redundancy

rationale: the two CNIs work together: Cilium handles packet processing, Services and policies; Kube-OVN handles the overlay network, IPAM, persistent IPs and VPC.

stem: What happens to a Service of type `LoadBalancer` in a bare-metal cluster **without** MetalLB?

options.text: It gets an IP from the pod network
Its external IP stays pending forever
It automatically falls back to NodePort

rationale: on bare metal nothing hands out external IPs: without MetalLB the Service's external address just stays pending.

stem: What describes MetalLB's BGP mode?

options.text: A single node answers ARP requests for the service IP
Nodes advertise service IPs to physical routers as routes
It works only in public clouds

rationale: in BGP mode, nodes peer with physical routers and advertise service IPs as routes (since v1.5 the backend is FRR-K8s); answering ARP is L2 mode.

stem: How is ingress deployed in Cozystack?

options.text: One shared ingress controller for the whole platform
One ingress-nginx controller per tenant, enabled by a tenant toggle
Ingress runs on a dedicated hardware appliance
Ingress is not supported; there are only Services of type LoadBalancer

rationale: ingress-nginx is deployed per tenant via the `ingress` toggle; if a tenant has none of its own, the service is inherited from the parent (M2).

stem: What does the TenantGateway data plane run on?
rationale: TenantGateway is the Gateway API as implemented by Cilium; there is no nginx anywhere in this data path.

stem: A tenant needs a wildcard certificate for `*.apps.example.com`. Which validation method makes this possible?
rationale: Wildcard certificates are issued only through DNS-01 validation. HTTP-01 does not issue them.

stem: The platform domain is `cloud.example.com`. What default domain will tenant `alpha`, created directly under the root, get?
rationale: A tenant's default domain is built as `<name>.<parent-domain>`, so alpha under the root gets `alpha.cloud.example.com`.

stem: Which component creates DNS records for published applications on its own?
rationale: ExternalDNS watches published services and ingresses and creates DNS records for them. cert-manager deals with certificates, not names.

stem: Which component stores metrics in Cozystack?
rationale: Metrics are stored by VictoriaMetrics (VMCluster). There is no Prometheus in the stack, only PromQL compatibility.

stem: A tenant has no Monitoring application of its own. What happens to monitoring of its workloads?

options.text: The tenant must install Prometheus by hand
The tenant uses the parent tenant's monitoring
The platform will refuse to run new workloads

rationale: Monitoring is a catalog application, one per tenant. If a tenant has none of its own, the nearest ancestor's monitoring is used: the usual inheritance rule from M2.

stem: Which component groups alerts and removes duplicates before notifications are sent?
rationale: The chain is: VMAlert evaluates the rules, Alerta groups, deduplicates and routes, and then on to Email/SMS/Slack.

stem: You need to check the state of LINSTOR volumes. Which group of standard dashboards should you open?
rationale: The Storage dashboard group shows the state of LINSTOR and SeaweedFS.

stem: A user wants a managed PostgreSQL database backed up automatically every night. Which object do they create?
rationale: A Plan is a scheduled (cron) backup. A BackupJob is a one-off run, and a Backup is the finished result.

stem: Which object exists at cluster level and is created by the platform administrator?
rationale: BackupClass is the only cluster-level object, and the platform administrator creates it. The rest are created by users or by the system itself.

stem: What does the `cozy-default` BackupClass provide in v1.5?

options.text: Automatic backups of the entire management cluster
A ready-made configuration with a shared system S3 bucket, so managed application backups work without administrator setup
A free external S3 account for every tenant

rationale: cozy-default ships out of the box starting with v1.5 and brings a shared system S3 bucket, so managed application backups are taken without administrator setup.

stem: Since which release has Velero been included in Cozystack by default?
rationale: Velero (cozystack.velero) became a standard platform component in v1.5.

stem: Which Velero object defines *where* backups are stored?
rationale: BackupStorageLocation describes the S3 storage that backups go to. Strategy defines how to back up, and BackupClass ties all of this to application types.

stem: What is NOT included in a data-only backup of a managed application? (Choose the most accurate answer.)

options.text: The Helm release, the application CR and the operator secrets
The contents of the S3 bucket
The Backup object with the result

rationale: Such a backup captures only the database contents. The Helm release, the application CR and the operator secrets are not part of it.

stem: Which condition must be met before restoring a managed application backup?

options.text: The target application must already be deployed
The tenant must be deleted first
Prometheus must be running in the cluster

rationale: A restore loads data into an existing database. Backups contain only data, so the target application must be deployed beforehand.

stem: What kind of virtual machine backups does the platform take?

options.text: Full: the configuration and all attached disks

rationale: A backup includes the configuration and all attached disks, and every backup is full: there are no incremental backups or CBT here.

stem: What does a controller do in Kubernetes?

options.text: Executes user commands one by one
Continuously compares the desired state with the actual state and fixes any drift
Stores the cluster configuration on disk

rationale: A controller runs a reconciliation loop: it compares the desired state with the actual state and closes the gap, over and over, forever.

stem: Which object provides a stable network name for a set of pods?
rationale: A Service provides a stable name and a virtual IP in front of a set of pods that keeps changing.

stem: Why does `kubectl get tenants` work in a Cozystack cluster?

options.text: Tenant is a built-in Kubernetes object type
Cozystack extends the Kubernetes API, and the API server knows the Tenant type (served by the cozystack-api aggregated server)
kubectl has a special Cozystack plugin
It only works in the dashboard terminal

rationale: Cozystack extends the Kubernetes API: the types in apps.cozystack.io are served by the cozystack-api aggregated API server, so ordinary kubectl commands work with them.

stem: Which API group holds the Cozystack catalog resources?
rationale: All catalog resources, Tenant, Postgres, VMInstance and the rest, live in apps.cozystack.io/v1alpha1.

stem: Which command do you start with to check the overall health of a Cozystack platform?
rationale: Every platform component is a HelmRelease, so `kubectl get hr -A` with READY True everywhere is the universal health check.

stem: What does a HelmRelease object describe?

options.text: A one-off install command that runs and disappears
That a specific chart with specific values must be installed and stay installed
A backup of a Helm chart
A Git repository with the application source code

rationale: A HelmRelease describes the desired state (chart, version, values), and FluxCD makes sure it all stays installed and matches the description.

stem: What is a Helm chart?

options.text: A running instance of an application
A package of Kubernetes manifest templates and metadata

rationale: A chart is a package: templates plus metadata. A release is that same chart installed with specific values.

stem: How is the Cozystack platform itself installed?

options.text: By copying binaries to all nodes over SSH
With a Helm command that installs the cozy-installer chart

rationale: The platform is installed with a single idempotent Helm command: `helm upgrade --install ... cozy-installer` into the cozy-system namespace (M1).
